findings.title: Watch goroutine never exits after backend channel close
findings.body: In search.init(), the watch goroutine uses `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }`. When the storage backend stops (e.g., via sql backend's `defer close(stream)` after `b.done` triggers), the channel is closed and `<-events` returns the zero value (a nil *WrittenEvent) forever. handleEvent then hits the `!slices.Contains(...)` branch and logs `ignoring watch event type 0` on every iteration, leading to unbounded log spam and a leaked goroutine for the lifetime of the process. The loop should be `for v := range events` (which exits when the channel closes) or use a `select` on a done channel. Combined with `watchctx := context.Background()` (which never cancels), there is no way to stop this goroutine. The PR's introduction of eager Init makes this more likely to be exercised during normal shutdown.

findings.title: Trace propagation fix is incomplete for the watch loop
findings.body: The PR description states 'Fixes trace propagation by passing span contexts down', but the long-running watch goroutine spawned in search.init() still uses `watchctx := context.Background()` (note the `// new context?` comment, suggesting this was intentionally left undone). The init() and build() functions now correctly propagate the new ctx via `ctx, span := s.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`, but the watch loop and everything downstream of it (all handleEvent invocations) lose the trace context. Either fix this to use the parent ctx for trace propagation, or document in the commit message why watch events are intentionally not traced.

findings.title: NewResourceServer now blocks on initialization, behavior change
findings.body: NewResourceServer now synchronously calls `s.Init(ctx)` before returning, which performs lifecycle init, builds the entire search index across all namespaces, and starts the watch loop. Previously this was deferred to the first gRPC call. Callers that constructed the server (e.g., tests, alternate wiring code) expecting non-blocking construction, or that supplied their own timeout for init, will now block indefinitely on a potentially expensive operation with no timeout context. The PR description asks 'Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily? What could this break?' but no callers were audited in the diff. At minimum, the timeout/context contract of NewResourceServer has changed and any test or production path that wanted to construct a server without paying the init cost will be affected.

findings.title: Search watch goroutine is leaked on partial init failure
findings.body: Init now runs: lifecycle.Init -> search.init -> initWatcher. search.init spawns the long-running watch goroutine (the one with the closed-channel bug above). If search.init succeeds but initWatcher then fails (returning the error from NewResourceServer), the watch goroutine is never torn down and the server is returned as nil to the caller, so nothing in the caller path can cancel it. There is no rollback or cleanup if a later init step fails after an earlier one has started goroutines. This needs either an explicit cleanup step or defer-with-undo pattern to release resources on partial init failure.

findings.title: BuildIndex span context is not propagated, inconsistent with other trace fixes
findings.body: The PR changes `_, span := ...Start(ctx, ...)` to `ctx, span := ...Start(ctx, ...)` in search.init, search.build, and sql.GetResourceStats to propagate the new ctx to downstream calls. bleve.BuildIndex still has `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")` and never reassigns ctx, so the new ctx (with the span) is discarded. This is inconsistent with the stated goal of fixing trace propagation. Either change this to `ctx, span := ...` for consistency, or note that BuildIndex has no child spans (and the discrepancy is intentional). Note also that the surrounding `_, err := index.NewBatch()`-style code creates side effects (a batch is opened); if any future code adds tracing to those paths it would silently miss the parent context.

findings.title: Stop writes s.initErr without synchronization
findings.body: Stop assigns `s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping")` outside of any mutex or sync.Once, while Init reads it under once.Do. After the PR, in practice the calls don't overlap (Init runs synchronously inside NewResourceServer and returns before Stop is reachable), but the field is still shared mutable state guarded only by `s.once` for reads in Init. A future change that calls Init externally (the once.Do machinery is still there, suggesting that was the intent) would race with Stop. Consider removing the s.initErr mutations in Stop entirely or guarding the field with a mutex.

findings.title: Postgres skip is a workaround, not a fix
findings.body: The diff adds `if dbType == "postgres" { t.Skip(...) }` with a TODO, but this PR directly changes the unified storage init path that the test exercises (the test boots the storage server target, which now eagerly calls Init inside NewResourceServer). The exact reason the test fails on postgres is unknown and unfixed, and the new init-at-startup behavior is not validated against postgres. The PR's main goal (fixing context-cancelled errors from lazy init) should be covered by a test that exercises the storage server target under at least one DB, not just mysql.
